result: The authors successfully established multi-view LSFM imaging protocols for Parhyale embryos, enabling long-term imaging at cellular resolution. Transgenic embryos with H2B-mRFPruby-labeled nuclei were imaged for 4-5 days, generating >7 TB datasets with >1 million images, using optimized parameters including 7.5 min intervals, periodic heat-shock for fluorescence replenishment, and multi-view acquisition.
evaluation: Claims C14-C16 and C72-C78 provide comprehensive methodological details and demonstrate successful long-term imaging. The imaging parameters are well-documented (C73, C75, C76), quality control was performed (C78), and the resulting data characteristics are quantified (C15, C83). The slow developmental tempo of Parhyale (C16) enabled the multi-view approach with minimal nuclear displacement between views.

result: The authors developed MaMuT (Massive Multi-view Tracker), a novel software tool for manual cell tracking in large multi-dimensional datasets. MaMuT integrates BigDataViewer and TrackMate, enables synergistic annotation from multiple views, and was used to reconstruct the complete T2 limb lineage requiring ~10 weeks of manual tracking by an expert annotator.
evaluation: Claims C24-C26 and C84-C86 establish MaMuT's technical foundation and capabilities. The software is openly available (C25, C26), handles up to ~100,000 annotations efficiently (C117), and enabled comprehensive lineage reconstruction (C86). The time investment (C71, C114) and advantages of manual tracking (C115, C116) are clearly documented. The unique multi-view annotation capability (C85) is a key innovation.

result: Complete single-cell lineage reconstruction of the Parhyale T2 limb (limb#1) was achieved by tracking 34 founder cells over 50 hours, generating 361 epidermal cells. The limb developed from rows b, c, d of E4 parasegment and rows a, b of E5 parasegment, with dramatic variation in division rates (1-5 differential divisions). This represents the most comprehensive lineage tree for any developing arthropod limb to date.
evaluation: Claims C27-C32 provide detailed quantitative lineage data with clear spatial and temporal resolution. The parasegmental origin (C27, C28), spatial distribution (C29), complete tracking statistics (C30, C31), and comparison to prior work (C32) are well-documented. The claim of being the most comprehensive arthropod limb lineage (C32) is supported by comparison to previous dye injection studies.

result: Digital clonal analysis revealed early lineage restrictions in the developing Parhyale limb along both AP and DV axes. A straight AP boundary separated anterior (E4b,c,d) from posterior (E5a,b) cells throughout development. A DV boundary was identified at the 4-row-parasegment stage, running between E4b/c rows anteriorly, E5a/b rows posteriorly, and through specific medial cells. These boundaries formed four compartments (AD, AV, PD, PV) with no cell mixing, confirmed in an independent limb#2 reconstruction.
evaluation: Claims C33-C36 demonstrate lineage restrictions through comprehensive cell tracking data. The AP boundary (C33) is consistent with known parasegmental organization. The DV boundary (C34, C35) is a novel finding supported by detailed spatial mapping and confirmed in an independent reconstruction (C36). The in silico approach (C87) provides insights not previously accessible in species lacking genetic lineage tracing tools.

result: Analysis of founder cell birth sequences confirmed that the second mitotic wave creating the 4-row-parasegment propagated from anterior to posterior rows and medial to lateral columns, with some variability between limbs. Despite imaging at different temperatures (26°C vs 29-30°C), the two limbs showed similar growth patterns after temporal rescaling by a factor of 1.6, with highly reproducible cell numbers up to 35 hours after the first tracked division.
evaluation: Claims C37-C41 provide quantitative temporal analysis of cell division patterns. The general anterior-to-posterior, medial-to-lateral progression (C37) is confirmed with noted deviations (C38, C39). The temporal rescaling approach (C40) successfully aligned growth curves from different temperatures, demonstrating reproducibility (C41). The variability noted (C39) is appropriately acknowledged.

result: Limb bud formation involved remodeling of flat epithelium into a 3D bulge through a stereotyped sequence: initial rise of cells at the four-compartment intersection (~96h AEL), followed by large-scale elevation of dorsal compartment cells within 3 hours. The AP/DV boundary intersection marked the limb tip throughout elongation. The limb elongated as a convoluted S-shaped cylinder rather than a straight structure.
evaluation: Claims C42-C46 and C88 describe the morphogenetic process with clear temporal and spatial resolution. The initial cellular events (C42, C43), boundary dynamics (C44), and morphological progression (C45, C46) are documented with specific timepoints and supported by figure references. The 3D epithelial remodeling (C88) is directly observed through the imaging data.

result: Quantitative analysis revealed striking spatial patterns in cell proliferation rates. Central cells divided faster than peripheral cells (average CCL 7.1-8.5 hr vs 8.5-16.4 hr), starting from the 4-row-parasegment stage. During elongation, fast-dividing cells concentrated at the distal tip (resembling a growth zone) and along the anterior AP boundary. Hierarchical clustering identified three distinct cell groups based on division patterns, with homologous cells between limb#1 and limb#2 showing significantly more similar division patterns (median 19.3% difference) than non-homologous cells.
evaluation: Claims C47-C53 provide rigorous quantitative analysis of cell proliferation with specific measurements and statistical comparisons. The spatial patterns (C47-C50) are clearly defined with quantitative CCL values. The clustering analysis (C51) and pairwise comparisons (C52, C53) demonstrate reproducibility between limbs with appropriate statistical testing. The association between differential proliferation and limb outgrowth (C48) is appropriately presented as suggestive rather than causal.

result: Analysis of mitotic spindle orientations revealed temporal changes in division patterns. Early divisions were strictly longitudinal (parallel to AP axis), but became more heterogeneous after the 4-row-parasegment. During limb bud formation and elongation, an increasing number of mitotic spindles aligned along the proximal-distal axis. These findings suggest that Parhyale limb outgrowth is driven by at least two patterned cell behaviors: differential proliferation rates and orderly spindle arrangement.
evaluation: Claims C54-C57 document division orientation patterns with clear temporal progression. The strict early longitudinal orientation (C54), subsequent heterogeneity (C55), and progressive PD alignment (C56) are quantified with rose diagrams showing percentages. The conclusion (C57) appropriately integrates proliferation and orientation data, though it is presented as a suggestion rather than definitive proof of causation.

result: Cell fate mapping along the proximal-distal axis showed that cells giving rise to proximal, medial, and distal limb segments occupied distinct positions in the germband grid at the 4-row-parasegment and in the early limb bud. When the limb split into two elements, the proximal element formed coxa, basis, and ischium, while the distal element formed merus, carpus, propodus, and dactylus. Distal segments originated from a disc of cells centered at the four-compartment intersection (E4c4-c6, E4d3-d6, E5a3-a6), and distal cells remained separate from proximal cells at the ischium/merus joint, suggesting secondary lineage restrictions along the PD axis.
evaluation: Claims C58-C61 provide detailed spatial mapping of segment origins with specific cell identities. The distinct positional origins (C58), element-to-segment relationships (C59), and cellular composition of distal segments (C60) are clearly documented. The suggestion of secondary lineage restrictions (C61) is appropriately tentative and supported by citation to similar findings in Drosophila.

result: Gene expression analysis validated cellular models of limb patterning. Ph-dpp expression localized to presumptive dorsal rows (E4c, E4d, E5a) at 84-96h AEL, with expression fading in medial columns and the border at column 4 descendants. By 96-108h AEL, strong Ph-dpp expression concentrated in anterior-dorsal cells abutting the AP boundary. Ph-Doc was detected in a subset of Ph-dpp-expressing cells initially, then co-localized with Ph-dpp at the AP boundary. Cells expressing Ph-dpp and Ph-Doc exhibited the highest proliferation rates, providing correlative evidence for morphogen-dependent growth control.
evaluation: Claims C62-C67 integrate gene expression with cellular lineage data. The spatial localization of Ph-dpp (C62, C63, C64) and Ph-Doc (C65, C66) is mapped onto reconstructed cell identities with cellular resolution. The correlation with proliferation rates (C67) is appropriately presented as correlative rather than causal. The graded expression and boundary limitations are acknowledged (C62).

result: Ph-H15 expression validated the predicted DV compartment boundary. Ph-H15 transcripts were detected specifically in b row cells, with expression initiating shortly after ab cells divided into a and b daughters at the 4-row-parasegment. Although initially activated in all b cells, Ph-H15 expression later faded in medial columns and persisted only in ventral limb cells near the body wall.
evaluation: Claims C68-C70 demonstrate precise spatial and temporal correlation between Ph-H15 expression and the predicted ventral cell identity. The b-row specificity (C68), timing relative to cell division (C69), and dynamic expression pattern (C70) all match predictions from the lineage analysis. This provides independent validation of the DV boundary model.

result: The Parhyale limb conforms to Meinhardt's boundary model, where a secondary developmental field (the PD axis) initiates and is patterned around the intersection of AP and DV compartment boundaries. The intersection of these boundaries was located at the limb tip and persisted in this position throughout elongation.
evaluation: Claims C89, C90, and C44 connect the observed cellular organization to an established theoretical framework. The persistent localization of the AP/DV boundary intersection at the limb tip (C44) directly supports the boundary model (C90). However, the claim that Parhyale "perfectly" conforms (C89) may be overstated given that only morphological/positional evidence is provided without functional validation.

result: The findings implicate growth-based morphogenesis as a driving mechanism for arthropod limb evagination. Differential cell proliferation between central (faster) and peripheral (slower) regions of the limb primordium, starting from early specification and becoming pronounced during limb bud elevation, suggests a causal association with limb outgrowth. This mechanism has been the dominant hypothesis for vertebrate limb outgrowth for 50 years but has never been implicated in arthropod limb evagination, though pharmacological inhibition of proliferation can reduce limb bud formation in Artemia.
evaluation: Claims C91-C93 establish the historical context, and C48 provides correlative evidence for the association between differential proliferation and limb outgrowth. However, the causal relationship is only suggested, not demonstrated. No functional experiments (e.g., proliferation inhibition in Parhyale) are presented to test causality. The Artemia example (C93) supports plausibility but is from a different species. Claim C94 appropriately characterizes this as demonstrating "functionally interdependent mechanisms" rather than proving causation.

result: Analysis of dpp, Doc, and H15 expression in Parhyale suggests conserved roles for these genes in dorsal and ventral cell fate specification, providing independent support for a compartment-based mechanism to pattern the DV axis of arthropod limbs. In Drosophila, Dpp and Wg ligands are induced at the AP boundary in dorsal and ventral cells respectively, creating concentration gradients that pattern the PD axis through limb gap genes and control DV cell fate through T-box selector genes. The PD expression of limb gap genes is conserved in arthropods including Parhyale.
evaluation: Claims C95-C98 establish the Drosophila paradigm with appropriate citations. Claim C99 appropriately presents the Parhyale findings as "suggesting" conservation rather than proving it. The gene expression patterns are consistent with conserved roles, and the compartment-based mechanism is supported by both lineage and expression data. However, functional validation would be needed to definitively establish conservation of gene function.

result: The authors anticipate that LSFM imaging and tracking approaches, combined with CRISPR/Cas-based genome editing, will provide tools to explore how morphogens regulate growth and form at cellular resolution. The stereotyped organization of Parhyale ectoderm will enable comparison of lineages, cell behaviors, and genes between serially homologous structures within and across embryos and malacostracan crustaceans.
evaluation: Claims C100 and C102 present reasonable future directions based on the established methods and biological features of Parhyale. The integration of LSFM/tracking with CRISPR/Cas (C100, citing Kao et al., 2016) is technically feasible. The stereotyped organization enabling comparative studies (C102) is well-supported by the current data and extensive citations. These are appropriately framed as anticipated future applications rather than current results.

result: Parhyale hawaiensis is a direct-developing crustacean with favorable biological and optical properties for developmental imaging studies. The body plan is specified during 10 days of embryogenesis, each embryo develops diverse specialized appendages along the AP axis, and eggs are 500 µm long with transparent eggshells, low autofluorescence, and low light scattering. The tempo and mode of development has important ramifications for imaging and tracking.
evaluation: Claims C1-C5 establish the biological rationale for using Parhyale, supported by appropriate citations (C1, C2) and direct measurements (C3-C5). These properties are well-documented in the literature and confirmed by the successful imaging results. Claim C101 appropriately connects these properties to the technical feasibility of the approach.

result: Light-sheet Fluorescence Microscopy (LSFM) is an ideal technology for studying tissue and organ formation in intact embryos, enabling capture of fast dynamic processes at high spatiotemporal resolution over long periods with minimal photobleaching and damage. Multi-view LSFM allows computational reconstruction with isotropic resolution. Software solutions exist for registration, fusion, and visualization, but automated cell segmentation and tracking do not yet reach the precision required for unsupervised lineage extraction.
evaluation: Claims C6-C10 provide appropriate background on LSFM technology and computational tools, all supported by extensive citations to the relevant literature. The limitation of automated tracking (C10) is well-documented in the cited literature and motivates the development of MaMuT. These claims establish the technical context for the study.

result: The authors establish the comparative context for arthropod limb development, contrasting Drosophila with other arthropods including Parhyale. In Drosophila, limb development occurs across embryonic, larval, and pupal stages in flat imaginal discs, with AP compartmentalization during embryogenesis and DV during larval development. In most other arthropods including Parhyale, all limb developmental processes occur during embryogenesis in 3D epithelial outgrowths. The AP boundary is conserved across arthropods at parasegment interfaces, but the DV separation mechanism, timing, and position have remained unexplored at the cellular level due to lack of lineage tracing methodologies.
evaluation: Claims C11-C13 and C103-C110 provide comprehensive comparative context supported by extensive literature citations. The distinctions between Drosophila and other arthropods (C103-C105) are well-established. The conservation of AP boundaries (C107, C108) and uncertainty about DV separation (C109, C110) appropriately frame the knowledge gap addressed by this study. The citations support all factual claims about prior work.

result: The authors document the overall developmental progression of Parhyale embryogenesis captured by LSFM. Segment formation occurred sequentially in AP progression. Appendage morphogenesis involved patterning, growth, and differentiation of ectodermal epithelial cells. Limbs were specified at ~3.5 days AEL and acquired definite morphology by ~8 days AEL through ventral bulging, PD elongation, and progressive segmentation. During germband formation, the ectoderm organized into a stereotyped grid with ordered AP rows (parasegments) and DV columns, with two rounds of longitudinal divisions and posterior addition of parasegments driving axial elongation.
evaluation: Claims C17-C23 describe the overall developmental progression with appropriate temporal landmarks and are supported by figure references and citations to prior work. These observations are consistent with established knowledge of Parhyale development and provide context for the detailed lineage analysis. The grid-like organization (C21) and parasegmental structure (C22) are well-documented in the cited literature.

result: A second T2 limb (limb#2) was imaged on a different LSFM system at 29-30°C and tracked using SIMI°BioCell software from a single view. The reconstruction was complete up to ~22 hours of imaging time (35 hours when scaled to limb#1 growth rate), after which increasing cell density and signal deterioration made tracking intractable, particularly for medial column descendants.
evaluation: Claims C79-C82 document the methods and limitations for the second limb reconstruction. The different imaging conditions (C79), tracking software (C80), completeness (C81), and limitations (C82) are clearly stated. This independent reconstruction provided validation for the limb#1 findings despite being less complete. The limitations are appropriately acknowledged.

result: The authors conclude that reconstruction of cell lineages and behaviors provides solid predictions and powerful contexts to study gene expression and function. By combining light-sheet microscopy with new tracking software, they revealed cellular architecture and dynamics underlying epithelial remodeling and organ morphogenesis in a non-conventional model. Expression of Distal-less, an early limb specification marker, is first detected at the 4-row-parasegment in cells at the AP/DV boundary intersection.
evaluation: Claims C111-C113 provide appropriate summary statements. The Distal-less expression pattern (C111) is supported by citations and consistent with the boundary model. The conclusions about the value of lineage reconstruction (C112) and the achievement of the study (C113) are justified by the comprehensive data presented. These represent appropriate synthesis of the findings.
